nameStory: Green ash gets its name from the green tinge on the underside of its leaves and young twigs, which helps distinguish it from its cousins like white ash and black ash. The scientific name 'pennsylvanica' honors Pennsylvania, where early botanists first formally described this widespread North American native.
description: Green ash is a medium to large deciduous tree that can reach 50-60 feet tall with a rounded crown. It's one of our most adaptable native trees, thriving in both wet and dry conditions across New England. The tree has compound leaves made up of 5-9 leaflets arranged like fingers on a hand, and produces distinctive winged seeds called samaras that helicopter down in fall.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Compound leaves with 5-9 oval leaflets arranged opposite each other along the stem, plus one at the tip. The leaflets have a slightly fuzzy, soft texture underneath with a subtle green tinge that gives the tree its name.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Distinctive paddle-shaped winged seeds (samaras) about 1-2 inches long that hang in clusters. The wing extends all the way down to the seed body, unlike maple seeds which have wings on both sides.

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Gray to brown bark with a distinctive diamond-shaped ridge pattern on mature trees. Young bark is smoother with a grayish color, developing the characteristic furrowed diamond pattern as it ages.

idTips.label: Buds
idTips.description: Dark brown to rusty-colored buds that are slightly fuzzy to the touch and arranged directly opposite each other on the twigs. The terminal bud (at the tip) is noticeably larger than the side buds.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Medium to large tree with a rounded, somewhat irregular crown. Branches grow opposite each other (not alternating), and the tree often has a straight trunk with ascending branches.

habitat: Green ash is remarkably adaptable, growing in wet floodplains, swampy areas, and stream banks, but also thriving in drier upland sites and disturbed soils. In New England, you'll find it along rivers, in bottomland forests, and increasingly in urban areas where it tolerates pollution and compacted soil. It often grows alongside silver maple, American elm, and cottonwood in wet areas, or with oaks and hickories on drier sites.

seasonality.spring: Small, inconspicuous purplish-green flowers appear in clusters before the leaves emerge in early spring. New leaves unfold in late April to early May with a fresh, bright green color.
seasonality.summer: Full compound leaves create dense shade, and you can easily see the green tinge on leaf undersides. This is when the tree is most recognizable by its foliage characteristics.
seasonality.fall: Leaves turn yellow (sometimes with hints of brown) before dropping, and the winged seeds ripen and begin falling, spinning like helicopter blades. Seeds are most noticeable and diagnostic in early fall.
seasonality.winter: Identified by opposite branching pattern, diamond-patterned bark on mature trees, and rusty-brown fuzzy buds. Persistent seed clusters may still hang from branches.

funFact: Green ash trees can actually change sex! Individual trees may produce only male flowers one year, only female flowers another year, or sometimes both types of flowers in the same season, making each tree's gender identity surprisingly fluid.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with white ash, but green ash has fuzzy leaf undersides with a green tinge while white ash has smooth, whitish leaf undersides. Remember: 'Green ash is fuzzy underneath, white ash is white underneath.' Black ash grows in wetter areas and has leaflets that attach directly to the main stem without individual stalks.
contextualKnowledge: Green ash populations have been devastated by the emerald ash borer, an invasive beetle that has killed millions of ash trees across North America since the early 2000s. Many of the green ash trees you see in New England today may be treated with insecticides or are in areas the beetle hasn't reached yet.
compareHints: Green ash differs from white ash by its fuzzy, green-tinged leaf undersides (white ash has smooth, whitish undersides) and its greater tolerance for wet soils. Unlike black ash, which grows almost exclusively in swamps, green ash thrives in both wet and dry conditions. European ash, occasionally planted in New England, has black buds instead of the rusty-brown buds of our native ashes.

relatedSpecies.distinction: White ash differs from black ash by preferring drier, upland sites (black ash loves wet areas) and having leaflets with short stalks, while black ash leaflets attach directly to the main stem.
Black ash differs from white ash by its preference for wet habitats, darker bark, and leaflets that lack individual stalks (sessile).
European ash differs from our native ashes primarily in its black, velvety winter buds - white ash has brown buds, green ash has smaller brown buds, and black ash has dark but pointed buds.
